title: How the heart keeps blood moving
intro: The heart is a muscular pump linking the lungs and the rest of the body. Its chambers, valves, electrical system and own blood supply cooperate. A normal pulse alone does not prove that all these parts work normally.

sections.heading: The route
paragraphs: Blood returns from the body to the right side and goes to the lungs. Oxygen-rich blood returns to the left side and is pumped into the aorta to supply the body.

sections.heading: Valves and muscle
paragraphs: Valves guide one-way flow. The muscle relaxes to fill and contracts to eject blood; valve disease and weak pumping are related but different problems.

sections.heading: Timing
paragraphs: Electrical signals normally start in the sinus node and spread through a conduction system. Rhythm and pumping strength are not identical; an irregular beat needs interpretation in context.

sections.heading: The heart's own supply
paragraphs: Coronary arteries nourish the heart muscle. A blockage can damage muscle even while blood remains inside the chambers. Activity, blood pressure and medicines may change the workload.

sections.heading: Assessing symptoms
paragraphs: Examination, an electrocardiogram and ultrasound answer different questions. New persistent chest pressure, severe breathlessness, collapse or symptoms suggesting a heart attack need emergency help, not a smartwatch reassurance.

A diagram explains typical structure, not the cause of an individual symptom. Before a consultation, note when a change began, what brings it on and how it affects daily activities. Bring previous results and ask how the findings fit together.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira asks why ultrasound is needed after an electrocardiogram. She learns one examines structure and pumping, the other electrical activity.

examples.title: Another practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Arben has persistent chest pressure and sweating. He seeks emergency help even though his watch displays an ordinary pulse.
